Mental health

Bipolar disorder

Episodes of mania and depression: how to recognise them, long-term treatment and relapse prevention.

Medical review Alejandro Rosàs, family doctor

Need help now? In Spain, 024 is free and open 24 hours; in an emergency call 112. Elsewhere, contact your local helpline or emergency services. This text is for general information: it cannot diagnose and does not replace seeing a professional.

What it is

Bipolar disorder is a mood disorder in which, with periods of stability in between, there are episodes of:

  • Mania: elated or very irritable mood, high energy, less need for sleep, rapid speech, racing thoughts, grandiosity and risky behaviour, such as overspending. It lasts at least a week or requires admission.
  • Hypomania: similar but milder symptoms, without serious impairment.
  • Depression: as described in the depression dossier. It usually takes up more time than the highs.

Type I (with at least one manic episode) is distinguished from type II (hypomanias and depressions). It affects around 1–2% of the population, has a strong hereditary component and usually begins in early adulthood.

What it is not

It is not "changing mood often" or being temperamental. Episodes last days or weeks, not hours, and are a clear change from the person's usual self.

How it is assessed

A specialist makes the diagnosis from the clinical history, often with input from relatives, because the person may not remember hypomania or see it as a problem. Many people are first diagnosed with depression; that is why it is important always to ask about past episodes of elation.

Which interventions are studied

  • Mood stabilisers: lithium remains the reference treatment for preventing relapse and reduces suicide risk; some anticonvulsants and antipsychotics are also used. They require regular blood tests.
  • Antidepressants on their own can trigger mania, so they are used with caution and together with a stabiliser.
  • Psychoeducation, individually or in groups: learning to recognise early warning signs. It has been shown to reduce relapses and admissions.
  • Regular sleep and routines, and avoiding alcohol and drugs.
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy, family therapy and interpersonal and social rhythm therapy.

How to seek help

With possible mania, which the person often does not recognise, it is worth contacting the family doctor or mental health services early, or emergency services if there is risk. For suicidal thoughts, call 024 in Spain or your local crisis line.

How to support someone

During stable periods, agree on a crisis plan: which signs point to relapse, what to do and whom to call. Respect the person's autonomy, but don't ignore warning signs.

Myths to avoid

  • "People with bipolar disorder can't lead a normal life". With treatment, many work, study and have families.
  • "If you feel well, you can stop your medication". Stopping abruptly greatly increases the risk of relapse.
  • "Creativity depends on not being treated". There is no evidence that treatment substantially reduces it.

References

  1. Vieta, E. et al. (2018). Bipolar disorders. Nature Reviews Disease Primers, 4, 18008.
  2. Colom, F. et al. (2003). A randomized trial on the efficacy of group psychoeducation in the prophylaxis of recurrences in bipolar patients whose disease is in remission. Archives of General Psychiatry, 60(4), 402–407.
